# 1.6 Habituation: getting used to what is always there {#sec-habituation}

<div data-life="status" data-stage="1.6h"></div>

The animals of the previous stage learn which berries are bad. They also spend a large part of their life
standing in front of a bush that has no berries, biting at it. Nothing new is needed in the world to see what is
missing: an animal should stop responding to something that stays the same and keeps giving nothing.

This stage changes one thing, in the eyes.

## The biology: adaptation and habituation

Step into a room with a strong smell and after a few minutes it is gone. The smell is still there; the receptors
have stopped reporting it. Sensory neurons respond to *change*: to what differs from the recent past. A steady
input is the background, and the background carries no news. This is *sensory adaptation*.

*Habituation* is the same thing seen in behaviour. A snail that is touched pulls in its horns. Touch it again and
again and it stops bothering. It is the simplest kind of learning there is, older than learning by association,
and found in every animal that has been tested, including ones with a few hundred neurons.

## The circuit

No new cells. Each of the eyes' **look** inputs now keeps a slow average of what it has been seeing, over
roughly the last fifty ticks, and passes on the difference between what it sees now and that average.

Two things follow, both for the whole brain, because every neuron downstream of the eyes now gets the adapted
look:

- **What stays in view fades.** An animal that stands in front of a bush sees its look sink into the average. The
  appetitive cells, driven by that look, fall silent, and with them the urge to bite. The animal moves on.
- **What is unusual stands out.** All berry bushes look alike in most respects, and that shared part is nearly
  always in view, so it is nearly always in the average. What passes through is the part that differs: the colour
  of this bush. The previous stage needed a special rule so that a lesson about a poison berry would attach to its
  colour and not to berries in general. Here that rule is gone. The synapses learn from what the eyes pass on, and
  the eyes already pass on the difference.

<div data-life="brain" data-stage="1.6h"></div>

The world is the one of the previous stage, unchanged.

<div data-life="settings" data-stage="1.6h"></div>

## Results

The control is the brain of the previous stage, with eyes that do not adapt, in the same world.

The first generations of main are a step back. Every synapse the animals inherit was shaped by eyes that reported
the whole look, and now reports only the difference. The population has to re-tune before the change can pay.

### Is it used?

There is no group of neurons to silence here, since the change is in how the inputs work. The matching test is to
switch the adaptation off in the final population and let the same animals live in the same worlds again.

<div data-life="table" data-stage="1.6h" data-example="adaptation_off"></div>

The lesions of the regions are shown for completeness. `no_plasticity` and `us_pain` tell whether learning is
still used now that it has no special rule.
